problem_domains.description: Designing meaningful, systematic benchmarks to assess realistic performance of classical and quantum optimization algorithms on practically relevant instances.
problem_domains.quote:
VI. BENCHMARKS
Benchmarking can provide insights into realistic algo-
rithmic performance when purely analytical methods fail,
and it can provide new perspectives that motivate deeper
analytical studies.

problem_domains.description: The document focuses on benchmarking quantum and classical methods for solving optimization problems.
problem_domains.quote: In the following section, we focus on benchmarking goals related to understanding the potential of quantum computers for solving optimization problems in terms of a fair comparison.

problem_domains.problem: comparison of classical and quantum algorithms
problem_domains.description: The need to compare classical and quantum optimization algorithms to demonstrate quantum advantage.
problem_domains.quote: One of the main goals of benchmarking in the present context is the comparison of classical and quantum algorithms — aiming at demonstrating quantum advantage.

problem_domains.problem: tracking progress in hardware and algorithmic developments
problem_domains.description: Using benchmarks to monitor improvements in quantum hardware and optimization algorithms over time.
problem_domains.quote: Benchmarking may also be executed to track the progress in hardware developments (cf. Sec. VIA) as well as algorithmic improvements.

problem_domains.description: Determining how optimization algorithms scale with problem size and when they fail to provide good solutions.
problem_domains.quote: Furthermore, benchmarking can give us insights into an algorithm’s scaling behavior: Is there a problem scale at which algorithms fail to provide good solutions — possibly due to hardware limitations?

problem_domains.description: Deciding whether benchmarks should be defined on the original optimization problem or on a specific mathematical model.
problem_domains.quote: For benchmarks, it is therefore crucial to decide on the level a problem is defined: either model-independent, i.e., on the level of the original optimization problem, which allows different mathematical modeling methods, or model-dependent, i.e., on the level of a concrete mathematical model.

problem_domains.description: Using pre-processing to reduce problem size and complexity before applying optimization algorithms.
problem_domains.quote: The goal of pre-processing is to modify the problem in such a way that it allows the optimization algorithm to work more efficiently.

problem_domains.description: Choosing the best-suited hardware platform (classical or quantum, analog or digital) for a given optimization problem.
problem_domains.quote: Tailoring the choice of platform to the characteristics of the problem at hand – if possible – can lead to better outcomes. This approach aligns with the idea of platform-aware optimization, ensuring that the selected platform is optimally matched to the unique requirements of the problem being addressed.

problem_domains.description: Designing benchmarks that allow fair comparison between very different classical and quantum systems.
problem_domains.quote: To understand the advantages and disadvantages of different platforms for different optimization problems, performing cross-platform benchmarking is crucial. At the same time, such benchmarks pose a particular challenge, as they must allow a fair comparison between systems that can function very differently.

problem_domains.description: Choosing metrics (resource cost, run time, quality, problem complexity) that enable fair comparison of optimization solvers.
problem_domains.quote: Due to the technological differences between classical and quantum systems, the selection of a set of metrics that enable a fair comparison is crucial. The four main metric categories that suffice said criteria are resource cost, run time, quality, and problem complexity.

problem_domains.problem: identifying standardized quantum optimization benchmark problems
problem_domains.description: Finding model-independent problems that are hard for classical solvers but suitable for current and near-term quantum technologies.
problem_domains.quote: Next, we present a set of model-independent problems that show promise for establishing standardized quantum optimization benchmarks. The problems should be chosen sufficiently hard for state-of-the-art classical solvers to leave a margin for quantum methods but within an intermediate size range where current and/or near-term quantum technologies can be effectively deployed.

problem_domains.quote: Use case 3: Energy retailing with storage. Consider an energy retailer that delivers energy to end customers. The energy supplier buys energy from energy producers in advance, e.g., on the day-ahead energy trading market, in one-hour time intervals, where the electricity price depends on several factors such as energy demand, renewable energy generation, etc. Additionally, the energy supplier has access to an energy storage system, e.g., a fleet of EVs that act as a virtual power plant, that can accumulate energy when this is cheap, to later use it when energy demand is high. solution_approaches.location: Section II. QUANTUM ADVANTAGE & COMPLEXITY THEORY (Page 3, first paragraph after heading I–II transition)

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum optimization algorithms as additional tools complementing classical algorithms
solution_approaches.description: Quantum optimization algorithms are positioned as complementary tools that can improve performance on some problem instances and work in synergy with classical methods.
solution_approaches.quote:
While quantum optimization
algorithms will not necessarily improve the performance
for all problems, they provide additional tools with new
properties that can have significant impact and improve
performance for some problem instances and thus, im-
prove our overall capabilities in optimization.

solution_approaches.approach: Grover (Adaptive) Search
solution_approaches.description: An exact quantum optimization algorithm paradigm based on Grover-style search.
solution_approaches.quote:
There are multiple approaches that lead to exact quan-
tum optimization algorithms, such as Grover (Adaptive)
Search [97–99] and the Quantum Adiabatic Algorithm
(QAA).
solution_approaches.location: Section III. PARADIGMS IN THE DESIGN OF QUANTUM OPTIMIZATION ALGORITHMS (Page 9)

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum Imaginary Time Evolution (QITE)
solution_approaches.description: A lesser-known approach mentioned as another paradigm for quantum optimization algorithm design.
solution_approaches.quote:
There are lesser known approaches too, like
Quantum Imaginary Time Evolution (QITE) [100], but
much of the published work focuses on the more well-
known approaches.
solution_approaches.location: Section III. PARADIGMS IN THE DESIGN OF QUANTUM OPTIMIZATION ALGORITHMS (Page 9)

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum sampling for Metropolis-Hastings and MCMC
solution_approaches.description: Quantum circuits used to enhance classical sampling-based optimization subroutines such as Metropolis-Hastings and Markov-chain Monte Carlo.
solution_approaches.quote:
There have also been a number of works suggesting
that quantum sampling could be a useful subroutine
in a larger classical algorithm. For example, there are
quantum circuits for Metropolis-Hastings algorithms [88]
andquantumenhancementofMarkov-chainMonte-Carlo
(MCMC) algorithms [89, 90].
solution_approaches.location: Section II.C. Heuristics in Quantum Optimization (Page 8–9)

solution_approaches.approach: Grover Search for constrained discrete optimization
solution_approaches.description: Uses Grover Search with oracles for objective and constraints to mark feasible solutions and achieve quadratic speedup over brute force.
solution_approaches.quote: Like for unconstrained discrete optimization, we can leverage Grover Search to achieve a quadratic speedup over brute force search [101]. This requires not only an oracle for the objective function, but also one for each constraint such that we can mark all feasible solutions.
solution_approaches.location: Page 18, Section IV PROBLEM CLASSES & ALGORITHMS

solution_approaches.approach: quantum branch and bound algorithm
solution_approaches.description: Adapts Grover Search to branch-and-bound trees to accelerate classical branch-and-bound algorithms.
solution_approaches.quote: In [254], a quantum branch and bound algorithm is introduced that accelerates classical branch-and-bound algorithms. It is shown that it solves most instances of the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model to optimality with a high probability in time O(20.226n). The algorithm adapts Grover Search to be applicable to search branch-and-bound trees.
solution_approaches.location: Page 18, Section IV PROBLEM CLASSES & ALGORITHMS

solution_approaches.approach: constraint-preserving ansatz in VQAs (Dicke state, particle-preserving ansatz)
solution_approaches.description: Designs ansätze restricted to the feasible subspace, e.g., fixed Hamming weight via Dicke states or particle-preserving gates.
solution_approaches.quote: The most straight-forward approach is to design an ansatz that – in the noise-free case – is restricted to the feasible space. For instance, suppose a constraint that fixes the Hamming weight of feasible bit strings, i.e., the number of ones. Then, we can prepare as initial state a uniform superposition of all these feasible bit strings, i.e., a Dicke state [255]. Or, we can use a parametric iSWAP or a Givens rotation gate, like in a particle preserving ansatz in quantum chemistry [256], to construct an ansatz that only generates feasible bit strings.
solution_approaches.location: Page 18, Section IV PROBLEM CLASSES & ALGORITHMS

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum Alternating Operator Ansatz (QAOA’)
solution_approaches.description: Generalizes QAOA with mixers and initial states tailored to hard constraints, keeping objective structure and cheaper cost operators.
solution_approaches.quote: The Quantum Alternating Operator Ansatz (QAOA’) [257, 258] generalizes the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm to much wider classes of problems and encodings, in particular to problems with hard constraints.
solution_approaches.location: Page 18, Section IV PROBLEM CLASSES & ALGORITHMS

solution_approaches.approach: quantum Zeno dynamics for constraint enforcement
solution_approaches.description: Uses repeated projections via mid-circuit measurements and auxiliary qubits to keep the state in the feasible subspace.
solution_approaches.quote: Another approach is to leverage quantum Zeno dynamics to repeatedly project the state back to the feasible subspace [265]. This requires auxiliary qubits as well as projective mid-circuit measurements.
solution_approaches.location: Page 18, Section IV PROBLEM CLASSES & ALGORITHMS

solution_approaches.approach: unconstrained black box binary optimization
solution_approaches.description: Hides constraints inside a black-box objective with a general infeasibility metric, avoiding many explicit penalty terms.
solution_approaches.quote: Instead of handling constraints explicitly in the quantum circuit, unconstrained black box binary optimization [200] allows hiding constraints in the black box objective function.
solution_approaches.location: Page 18, Section IV PROBLEM CLASSES & ALGORITHMS

solution_approaches.approach: Iterative or Recursive QAOA variants for constraints
solution_approaches.description: Adapts iterative QAOA schemes to enforce constraints by variable fixing strategies.
solution_approaches.quote: Alternatively, Iterative or Recursive QAOA variants, cf. Sec. IVA1, may be adapted to enforce constraints as suggested in [230]. Here, as for the unconstrained case, problems are solved iteratively and usually one variable is removed at a time.
solution_approaches.location: Page 18, Section IV PROBLEM CLASSES & ALGORITHMS

solution_approaches.approach: QUBO-Plus
solution_approaches.description: Incorporates certain constraints natively rather than as penalties, leading to sparser QUBO instances.
solution_approaches.quote: This is sometimes called QUBO-Plus [266], i.e., QUBO plus special types of constraints.
solution_approaches.location: Page 18, Section IV PROBLEM CLASSES & ALGORITHMS

solution_approaches.approach: quantum MWU-based SDP solvers (Gibbs-state based first-order methods)
solution_approaches.description: Uses multiplicative weights update with Gibbs state preparation and trace inner products to solve SDPs and LPs.
solution_approaches.quote: The first quantum algorithms for SDPs were first order methods, based on the Multiplicative Weights Update (MWU) framework [272]. In this framework one uses candidate solutions X that are proportional to ρ = exp(∑m i=1 yiAi)/ tr(exp(∑m i=1 yiAi)) for some (sparse) vector y ∈ Rm.

solution_approaches.approach: quantum IPMs using quantum linear system solvers and tomography
solution_approaches.description: Accelerates Newton steps in interior point methods via quantum linear system algorithms followed by state tomography.
solution_approaches.quote: It is therefore natural to try to use quantum linear system solvers [140, 284] in an effort to accelerate the computation of the Newton step [285].
solution_approaches.location: Page 20, Section IV.B.1 Second order methods

solution_approaches.approach: QRAM-based quantum IPM with condition-number-free speedup for tall LPs
solution_approaches.description: Uses a quantum algorithm for spectral approximations of BᵀB to speed up IPMs for LPs with many more constraints than variables.
solution_approaches.quote: Very recently, a quantum speedup for interior point methods was achieved without introducing a dependence on a condition number [291]. Under some mild assumptions and access to QRAM, this IPM achieves a quantum speedup for linear programs in which the number of linear inequalities m is much larger than the number of variables n
solution_approaches.location: Page 20, Section IV.B.1 Second order methods

solution_approaches.approach: quantum SDP-solvers for MAXCUT via Gibbs state preparation
solution_approaches.description: Reduces MAXCUT SDP feasibility to preparing a Gibbs state with specific properties and uses MWU with specialized oracles.
solution_approaches.quote: Brandao et al. [181] demonstrated that, after normalizing the diagonal constraints by n and relaxing slightly the constraints, feasibility reduces the task of solving the MAXCUT SDP to a possibly simpler task: preparing a Gibbs state that is (i) approximately indistinguishable from the maximally mixed state when measured in the computational basis, and (ii) whose trace inner product with C is close to an estimate of the optimal objective value, determined via binary search.
solution_approaches.location: Page 20, Section IV.B.1 Quantum SDP-solvers for approximating MAXCUT

solution_approaches.approach: MAXCUT SDP via Quantum Singular Value Transformation-based Gibbs sampling
solution_approaches.description: Improves precision scaling and removes sparsity dependence using QSVT-based Gibbs sampling with QRAM.
solution_approaches.quote: Moreover, it is shown that when C is stored in QRAM, one can remove the dependence on the sparsity parameter by using Gibbs sampling techniques based on Quantum Singular Value Transformation [143].
solution_approaches.location: Page 20, Section IV.B.1 Quantum SDP-solvers for approximating MAXCUT

solution_approaches.approach: quantum algorithms for matrix scaling and balancing
solution_approaches.description: Applies first- and second-order quantum methods, including amplitude amplification and graph sparsification, to matrix scaling formulations.
solution_approaches.quote: Recent works [294, 297] have shown how to speedup both first- and second-order methods for a natural convex formulation of the problem, using a variety of techniques (basic amplitude amplification, but also graph sparsification).
solution_approaches.location: Page 20, Section IV.B.1 Quantum algorithms for matrix scaling and matrix balancing

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum Hamiltonian Descent (QHD)
solution_approaches.description: Quantizes continuous-time accelerated gradient descent by simulating a designed Hamiltonian whose ground state encodes the optimizer.
solution_approaches.quote: The first work in this line of research is Quantum Hamiltonian Descent (QHD) [298], which can be viewed as a quantization of the Bregman-Lagrangian framework for continuous-time accelerated gradient descent introduced by Wibisono et al. [299].
solution_approaches.location: Page 20-21, Section IV.B.1 Quantum approaches with no direct classical equivalent

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum Central Path Method (QCPM)
solution_approaches.description: Simulates a Hamiltonian whose ground state encodes the central path of an LP, avoiding QRAM and linear system solvers.
solution_approaches.quote: Along this line, Augustino et al. [300] describe a fully quantum algorithm for solving linear optimization problems by quantum-mechanical simulation of the central path, which the authors call the Quantum Central Path Method (QCPM).
solution_approaches.location: Page 21, Section IV.B.1 Quantum approaches with no direct classical equivalent

solution_approaches.approach: quantum algorithms for stochastic gradient descent in non-convex optimization
solution_approaches.description: Use quantum access to stochastic gradients to achieve improved query complexity for finding critical points.
solution_approaches.quote: On the other hand, Sidford and Zhang [305] show query upper bounds for finding critical points with quantum algorithms for stochastic gradient descent (SGD). With access to a probability-weighted superposition over the bounded-variance stochastic gradient, the algorithm requires O(√nϵ−3) queries

solution_approaches.approach: quantum gradient descent via amplitude encoding and quantum linear algebra
solution_approaches.description: Implements gradient descent steps as transformations on amplitude-encoded states using quantum linear systems and related methods.
solution_approaches.quote: In high-dimensional situations, the availability of the quantum linear systems algorithm and of quantum linear-algebra methods motivates the direct quantum implementation of gradient descent over O(polylog(n)) qubits [285, 306] to provide descriptions of stationary points of non-convex functions.

solution_approaches.approach: quantum simulated annealing and quantum walks for non-convex optimization
solution_approaches.description: Uses quantum walks and tunneling to speed up simulated annealing and SGD over rugged landscapes.
solution_approaches.quote: The idea of simulated annealing, finding global minima assisted by thermal fluctuations, applies to continuous non-convex optimization as well. Quantum computers obtain polynomial speedups in executing the classical simulated annealing process via quantum walks [308]. Quantum fluctuations provide an additional resource allowing quantum tunneling through barriers between different minima [309].

solution_approaches.approach: quantum ADMM / decomposition for MIP (QUBO subproblem on quantum computer)
solution_approaches.description: Solves QUBO subproblems quantumly within ADMM or decomposition frameworks while continuous parts are classical.
solution_approaches.quote: Decomposition/Splitting/ADMM: this is a large class of algorithms that is based on decomposing the problem. Refs. [317, 318] suggested solving the QUBO sub-problem using a quantum computer, while solving the continuous sub-problem classically.

solution_approaches.approach: quantum Benders decomposition
solution_approaches.description: Uses quantum methods within Benders decomposition for MIP, though guarantees are not yet established.
solution_approaches.quote: A similar approach has been tested by Chang et al. [319], in the context of Benders decomposition.

solution_approaches.approach: Lagrangian relaxation with quantum subroutines
solution_approaches.description: Applies Lagrangian relaxation where some subproblems or circuit-parameter optimizations are handled quantumly.
solution_approaches.quote: Another, approach that optimizes over the Lagrangian function classically over the circuit parameters and dual variables has been introduced by Le and Kekatos [321].

solution_approaches.approach: quantum-enhanced branch-and-bound for MIP
solution_approaches.description: Combines quantum speedups for convex relaxations and branching decisions to accelerate branch-and-bound-and-cut.
solution_approaches.quote: One possibility for a hybrid implementation is that discrete decisions are handled by branching and generation of cuts implemented classically, while the continuous, possibly convex relaxations could be solved on the quantum computer.

solution_approaches.approach: reformulation of MIP to high-dimensional LPs and SDPs with quantum solvers
solution_approaches.description: Uses Dantzig-Wolfe and moment/SOS reformulations to LP/SDP that can be attacked by quantum LP/SDP algorithms.
solution_approaches.quote: Reformulation to high-dimensional LPs: using techniques that go back to Dantzig and Wolfe [326], one can reformulate mixed-integer programs as in Eq. (13) as a very large linear program (LP).

solution_approaches.approach: completely positive / copositive reformulation with quantum cut generation
solution_approaches.description: Recasts MIP as LP over copositive cones and uses a quantum QUBO solver to generate cuts.
solution_approaches.quote: A mathematically elegant reformulation of a mixed-integer programming problem results in a linear program over the dual of the cone of copositive matrices [330]. ... This approach has been tried in [334], using a QUBO solver to generate cuts.

solution_approaches.approach: quantum dynamic programming with Grover search
solution_approaches.description: Combines classical DP for part of the state space with Grover search over remaining combinations to speed up exponential-time DP.
solution_approaches.quote: The quantum algorithms are a combination of classical dynamic programming and Grover’s search.

solution_approaches.approach: quantum DP for TSP and related problems
solution_approaches.description: Uses DP up to a subset size and then Grover search to combine partial solutions for TSP and other hypercube-structured problems.
solution_approaches.quote: For example, the quantum algorithm for TSP by Ambainis et al. [338] first uses DP to compute the shortest paths through sets of cities that contain up to 24% of all cities and then uses Grover’s search to find the shortest combination of those paths that visits all the cities and returns to the starting point.

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum optimization approaches for contextual multi-armed bandits, MDPs, and differential-equation-constrained problems
solution_approaches.description: Use quantum optimization algorithms to find global solutions to contextual bandits, MDPs, and optimization problems constrained by differential equations, thereby solving associated HJB equations.
solution_approaches.quote:
In what follows we discuss po-
tential quantum optimization approaches to find global
solutions to the three aforementioned problems:
1. Contextual multi-armed bandit problems.
2. Markov decision processes (MDPs).
3. Optimization problems constrained by differential
equations.
solution_approaches.location: Page 26, Section IV PROBLEM CLASSES & ALGORITHMS

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum-accelerated value iteration and policy iteration via convex optimization and quadratic speedup
solution_approaches.description: Apply quantum convex optimization methods and quadratic speedup techniques to value iteration and policy iteration formulations of MDPs.
solution_approaches.quote:
Potential algorithms include:
1. Value iteration and policy iteration boil down to
optimization problems, wherein the convex opti-
mization of Sec. IVB1 could be applicable, perhaps
combined with the quadratic speedup of approaches
of Sec. IVD.
solution_approaches.location: Page 26, Section IV PROBLEM CLASSES & ALGORITHMS

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum-accelerated reinforcement learning (LSTD and related) via convex optimization and tabular methods
solution_approaches.description: Use quantum convex optimization and tabular quantum methods to speed up reinforcement learning algorithms such as Least-Squares Temporal-Difference.
solution_approaches.quote:
2. Reinforcement learning is a broad family of ap-
proaches, rather than a single algorithm, which
approximate value or policy iteration, for instance
using Least-Squares Temporal-Difference (LSTD).
Again, the convex optimization of Sec. IVB1 could
be applicable, perhaps together with the tabular
method of Sec. IVD providing additional speedup.
solution_approaches.location: Page 26, Section IV PROBLEM CLASSES & ALGORITHMS

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum reinforcement learning with unitary oracular access
solution_approaches.description: Use quantum reinforcement learning algorithms with coherent, unitary access to the environment to achieve quadratic speedups in tasks like multi-armed bandits and optimal q-function estimation.
solution_approaches.quote:
3. Quantum reinforcement learning (heuristics). In
the unitary oracle setting, from the perspective of
exact methods, that is, algorithms that are guaran-
teed to identify optimal policies in arbitrary envi-
ronment, tight quantum upper and lower bounds
have been identified. In Refs. [350, 351], lower
bounds on the more special task of Multi-armed
bandit problems were found, along with essentially
matching quantum upper bounds, for a number of
RL-related tasks, including finding the optimal q-
function. These works achieve a quadratic speedup
over best possible classical methods, assuming ap-
propriate oracle access to the task environment.
solution_approaches.location: Page 26-27, Section IV PROBLEM CLASSES & ALGORITHMS

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum reinforcement learning with classical access and parameterized quantum circuits
solution_approaches.description: Develop parameterized-circuit-based quantum reinforcement learning algorithms that operate with classical access to the environment and can exhibit superpolynomial advantages under complexity assumptions.
solution_approaches.quote:
However, the second research line investigates quan-
tum enhancements in reinforcement learning when the
access to the task environment is restricted to be clas-
sical. Here too speedups are provably possible, at least
in special cases, but now subject to standard complex-
ity assumptions. For example in Refs. [357, 358] it was
proven that there exist task environments with a super-
polynomial advantage for quantum reinforcement learn-
ing algorithms (with respect to finding optimal policies
and optimal q-functions), unless the discrete logarithm
problem has an efficient classical solution. ... In this domain, there has been substantial effort
in defining various types of parameterized-circuit based
QRL algorithms [357, 361, 362].
solution_approaches.location: Page 27, Section IV PROBLEM CLASSES & ALGORITHMS

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum policy optimization with quadratic speedup
solution_approaches.description: Use quantum methods to obtain quadratic speedups in optimizing parameterized policies under certain regularity conditions.
solution_approaches.quote:
In Jerbi et al.[354] it was shown that quadratic speedups
in policy optimization were possible as long as the poli-
cies satisfy certain regularity conditions, which are, e.g.,
satisfied for policies defined by parameterized quantum
circuits.
solution_approaches.location: Page 27, Section IV PROBLEM CLASSES & ALGORITHMS

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum stopping time algorithm for American option pricing using Quantum Amplitude Estimation
solution_approaches.description: Given quantum access to a sampler of the underlying stochastic process, use Quantum Amplitude Estimation to obtain a polynomial speedup for pricing American options via optimal stopping.
solution_approaches.quote:
Given quantum ac-
cess to a sampler for the stochastic process, a quantum
algorithm with a polynomial speedup using Quantum
Amplitude Estimation (QAE) [169, 366] was shown by
Doriguello et al.[367].
solution_approaches.location: Page 27, Section IV PROBLEM CLASSES & ALGORITHMS

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum robust optimization via stochastic gradient and quantum sampling
solution_approaches.description: Extend classical meta-algorithms for robust optimization by using quantum access to functions, stochastic gradients, and quantum sampling subroutines to obtain polynomial advantage.
solution_approaches.quote:
Ben-Tal et al.[376] devel-
oped meta-algorithms to approximately solve the robust
version of a given optimization problem using an oracle
for the solving of the original optimization problem. A
quantum version was developed by Lim et al. [377], us-
ing quantum access to the functions, extending the origi-
nal algorithm to include a stochastic gradient, and using
quantum sampling subroutines with polynomial advan-
tage.

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum subroutines for Multi-Objective Optimization
solution_approaches.description: Apply quantum optimization subroutines or quantum state sampling to classical MOO strategies to approximate the efficient frontier.
solution_approaches.quote:
There is only very little literature considering quantum
optimization algorithms for MOO. Most of the proposals
apply classical strategies and use quantum optimization
sub-routines for the resulting single objective optimiza-
tion problems [382] or sample from quantum states to
approximate the efficient frontier [383].

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum convex optimization and MWU-based methods for MDPs
solution_approaches.description: Use quantum implementations of convex optimization and multiplicative weights update (MWU) methods to accelerate value iteration or LSTD sketches for MDPs.
solution_approaches.quote:
In the era of
noisy quantum computers, convex optimization algo-
rithms may be hard to use directly. Nevertheless, one
may considering sketching the value iteration [368] or
(LSTD) [369], wherein both the random projections and
the convex optimization could be implemented quan-
tumly. What MDPs could have a bound on the radius
of the ball outscribed to the (primal, dual) feasible set?
Such MDPs could benefit from speedup of quantum al-
gorithms based on MWU, cf. Sec. IVB1.
solution_approaches.location: Page 27, Section IV PROBLEM CLASSES & ALGORITHMS (open questions paragraph)

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum kernel-based value function approximation
solution_approaches.description: Approximate value functions using quantum kernels that encode inductive bias derived from continuous and discrete HJB structure.
solution_approaches.quote:
Approximat-
ing the value function, discrete or continuous, using the
concept of inductive bias recently introduced in the con-
text of function approximation by means of quantum ker-
nels [370]. Basic idea is to embed a prior knowledge of
certain properties of the value function into the design of
the approximator...
solution_approaches.location: Page 27, Section IV PROBLEM CLASSES & ALGORITHMS (open questions paragraph)

solution_approaches.approach: QAOA with warm-starts, constraint-preserving mixers, and counter-diabatic terms
solution_approaches.description: Optimize QAOA performance on noisy hardware by using warm-starts, mixers that encode constraints, and counter-diabatic terms while keeping circuit depth low.
solution_approaches.quote:
For exam-
ple, a warm-start reduces the number of QAOA lay-
ers [197, 198]. In addition, the QAOA mixer can be
changed to include constraints of the optimization prob-
lem[258,397], e.g., for equality constraints[259,260]. Al-
tering the mixer improves the approximation ratio com-
pared to penalty term constraints (soft constraints) for
constrained optimization problems [398]. Furthermore,
counter diabatic terms may also improve the approxi-
mation ratio [399].
solution_approaches.location: Page 29, Section V.A.1 Modeling, quantum algorithms, and encoding

solution_approaches.approach: Dense encodings via Quantum Random Access Codes (QRAC)
solution_approaches.description: Use QRACs to encode more classical decision variables into fewer qubits, trading off retrieval probability and approximation ratio.
solution_approaches.quote:
However, en-
coding schemes such as Quantum Random Access Codes
(QRAC) can encode m bits of information in n qubits
where m > n . ... As discussed in Sec. IVA1, this allows
the hardware to tackle problems with more decision vari-
ables than it has qubits [180, 237, 238, 410]. However,
denser encodings tend to have a lower approximation ra-
tio and introduce additional overhead to readout solution
candidates.
solution_approaches.location: Page 29-30, Section V.A.1 Modeling, quantum algorithms, and encoding

solution_approaches.approach: Transpilation optimizations including SWAP networks and structure-aware routing
solution_approaches.description: Use transpiler strategies that exploit problem structure (e.g., commuting two-qubit blocks in QAOA) and SWAP networks to reduce circuit depth on limited-connectivity hardware.
solution_approaches.quote:
For example, QAOA results in
circuits with blocks of commuting two-qubit gates. Ex-
ploiting this structure results in shallower quantum cir-
cuits [402, 418, 429–431]. More precisely, if the topol-
ogy of the problem graph does not perfectly match the
coupling map of the QPU, SWAP gates are necessary
to enable two qubit gates between unconnected qubits.
The denser the graph, the more SWAP gates are neces-
sary which results in a deeper circuit [402].

solution_approaches.approach: Dynamic circuits to address limited connectivity
solution_approaches.description: Use mid-circuit measurements and classically controlled operations (dynamic circuits) to implement constant-depth QAOA on grid-like coupling maps with auxiliary qubits.
solution_approaches.quote:
Modern hardware also exposes new circuit instructions
such as dynamic circuits [432]. In a dynamic circuit some
of the qubits are measured and the outcome of these
measurements changes the following circuit instructions
within the coherence time of the qubits. For instance,
this offers additional possibilities to address limited qubit
connectivity [433]. As an example, the SWAP based im-
plementation of the QAOA problem graph may be re-
placed on grid-like QPU coupling maps by constant depth
circuits with a quadratic auxiliary qubit overhead [434].

solution_approaches.approach: Error mitigation: Probabilistic Error Cancellation (PEC), Zero-Noise Extrapolation (ZNE), and PEA
solution_approaches.description: Apply PEC, ZNE, and probabilistic error amplification (PEA) to obtain noise-mitigated expectation values for quantum optimization circuits.
solution_approaches.quote:
Typically, most error mitigation methods,
such as Probabilistic Error Cancellation (PEC) [15] and
Zero-Noise Extrapolation (ZNE) [16, 439, 442], produce
noise-mitigated expectation values. ... This
prompted the development of PEA [16], a probabilistic
ZNE, in which the noise is learned like in PEC but then
amplified (instead of canceled) to then extrapolate to the
zero-noise limit.
solution_approaches.location: Page 31, Section V.A.3 Error suppression and mitigation

solution_approaches.approach: Error suppression via Dynamical Decoupling (DD)
solution_approaches.description: Insert DD pulse sequences in idle times of circuits to suppress non-Markovian errors without extra shots.
solution_approaches.quote:
Error suppression
methods reduce the noise in quantum circuits without
having to gather more shots. Most prominently, Dynam-
ical Decoupling (DD) suppresses non-Markovian errors
by adding pulses in idle times of a quantum circuit [435–
437].
solution_approaches.location: Page 31, Section V.A.3 Error suppression and mitigation

solution_approaches.approach: Pulse-efficient transpilation and pulse-level optimal control
solution_approaches.description: Use pulse-level compilation, including pulse-efficient transpilation and quantum optimal control, to reduce schedule duration and synthesize more efficient gates.
solution_approaches.quote:
Pulse control enables many different types of optimiza-
tions to reduce schedule durations. This may be as sim-
ple as a pulse-efficient transpilation in which variational
parameters are encoded in durations of cross-resonance
pulses [446]. ... Finally, advanced methods of quan-
tum optimal control can help synthesize gates [449, 450],
measurements [449, 451], and adiabaticity [120] which
may be useful in the context of approximate quantum
optimization.
solution_approaches.location: Page 31-32, Section V.A.4 Pulse-level and compiler

solution_approaches.approach: QAOA
solution_approaches.description: Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm used as a variational quantum algorithm for QUBO-type problems such as MAXCUT and Sherrington–Kirkpatrick.
solution_approaches.quote: Tab. IV summarizes existing quantum optimization hardware implementations run with (variants of) QAOA or VQE and problems corresponding either to (weighted) MAXCUT, Sherrington-Kirkpatrick, or other instances of QUBO/PUBO that use more than 15 qubits.

solution_approaches.approach: FVQE (filtering variational quantum eigensolver)
solution_approaches.description: A VQE variant applied to QUBO job shop scheduling problems on quantum hardware.
solution_approaches.quote: QUBO (JSP) FVQE 23 N/A 0.88 N/A 1 ≤ p ≤ 2 2022 [545]

solution_approaches.approach: QAMPA (quantum alternate mixer-phaser ansatz)
solution_approaches.description: A hardware-efficient ansatz derived from QAOA used for Sherrington–Kirkpatrick problems.
solution_approaches.quote: Sherrington-Kirkpatrick QAMPA 50 100 % 0.55 0.83 p = 2 2023 [264]

solution_approaches.approach: GQAOA (greedy QAOA)
solution_approaches.description: A greedy procedure that fixes several variables classically and solves a reduced problem with QAOA on quantum hardware.
solution_approaches.quote: The 72 qubit experiment by Dupont et al. [229] on the other hand, employs a greedy procedure. In each iteration cycle, several variables are set to values that are evaluated with a classical procedure, hence, producing a smaller optimization problem to be solved on the quantum computer.

solution_approaches.approach: NDAR-QAOA (noise-directed adaptive remapping)
solution_approaches.description: A meta-heuristic that adaptively gauge transforms the cost Hamiltonian to improve QAOA performance on noisy hardware.
solution_approaches.quote: Finally, the recently proposed Noise-Directed Adaptive Remapping meta-heuristic improves algorithm performance on noisy hardware by adaptively gauge transforming the cost Hamiltonian, with its effectiveness demonstrated for QAOA with 82 qubits [546].

solution_approaches.approach: QRAO

open_questions.question: Can better lower bounds for quantum speedups of generic DP algorithms be proved, and can good quantum approximations or heuristics be found?
open_questions.quote: Can we prove better lower bounds for quantum speedups of generic DP algorithms? In addition to provable algorithms, can we find good quantum approximations or heuristics, such as reinforcement learning?

open_questions.question: Can quantum stopping time algorithms based on QAE be extended to other problem classes and made more near-term friendly?
open_questions.quote:
Key questions are whether we can
extend such stopping time algorithms to other problem
classes and to problems with more decisions, and whether
we can make the algorithms more near-term quantum
friendly.

Looking forward, addi-
tional research on quantum tailored modeling of opti-
mization problems is needed to find the right balance
between model approximations and noise susceptibility.

Additional research is needed to see how to leverage dy-
namic circuits to reduce the circuit depth and width.

open_questions.question: How to design application-tailored benchmarks that fairly assess quantum optimization performance on realistic tasks?
open_questions.quote:
We foresee that more application
tailored benchmarks are needed, especially since many
algorithms are heuristic in nature.

open_questions.question: How to set up optimization competitions and libraries compatible with near-term quantum computers?
open_questions.quote:
Optimization competitions and libraries of this form
that are compatible with (near-term) quantum comput-
ers do not exist as of now. It remains an open task to set
them up and, thereby, enable streamlined benchmarking
of quantum optimization methods.

open_questions.question: At what problem scale do quantum and classical optimization algorithms fail to provide good solutions, and how do required resources scale with system size?
open_questions.quote: Furthermore, benchmarking can give us insights into an algorithm’s scaling behavior: Is there a problem scale at which algorithms fail to provide good solutions — possibly due to hardware limitations? How do the resources needed to find solutions to a problem of a certain quality scale with the system size?

open_questions.question: Can quantum algorithms better handle phase transition phenomena in SAT and related problems than classical algorithms?
open_questions.quote: It may now be of particular interest to investigate whether a quantum algorithm is better suited to handle the difficulty of a phase transition.

open_questions.question: For which ranges of problem parameters do computational phase transitions occur, and how do they affect optimization difficulty?
open_questions.quote: Understanding the range of problems and characteristics where phase transition behavior is observed presents a challenging task.

open_questions.question: Can quantum algorithms achieve superpolynomial speedups on spin glass problems that are average-case hard for classical algorithms?
open_questions.quote: It remains open as to whether quantum algorithms can do better in these average-case settings, and thus, superpolynomial speedups for spin glass problems are still possible.

open_questions.question: How to agree on common metrics and benchmarks for quantum optimization to enable comparable and fair evaluations?

open_questions.question: How to identify real-world optimization problems that are promising candidates for practically relevant quantum advantage?
open_questions.quote: Identifying optimization problems that are promising candidates for a practically relevant quantum advantage is challenging.

open_questions.question: How to effectively combine modeling and optimization to achieve practically relevant results for financial industry use cases?
open_questions.quote: The main challenge remains to effec- tively combine both the modeling and optimization of problems to achieve practically relevant results for in- dustry use cases.

open_questions.question: What additional directions (e.g., heavy-tailed distributions, Bayesian priors, non-Markovian processes) should be investigated for industry-specific quantum optimization applications?
open_questions.quote: However, there are many more di- rections to investigate, such as handling skewed, non- Gaussian heavy tailed probability distributions, Bayesian approaches and industry sector or subgroup specific pri- ors, or non-Markovian decision processes.

open_questions.question: How should clear benchmarks be established to reliably interpret scientific insights and identify quantum advantages?
open_questions.quote: Such considerations motivate the need to establish clear benchmarks, cf. Sec. VI, which enable a reliable interpretation of the scientific insights by a broader audience.
